questions.title: How exactly does the KL-constrained objective yield the closed-form optimal policy in Eq. (4)?
questions.question_body:
The paper claims that maximizing Eq. (3) (expected reward minus a KL to a reference policy) gives the optimal policy

$$\pi_r(y\mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\left(\frac{1}{\beta} r(x,y)\right).$$

I can guess this comes from a Lagrangian with a normalization constraint over $y$, but I'm getting lost in the steps: which terms are treated as constants when differentiating w.r.t. $\pi$? Could someone provide the explicit derivation from Eq. (3) to Eq. (4), including how the partition function $Z(x)$ arises and how the constraint $\sum_y \pi(y\mid x)=1$ is enforced?

questions.title: Why does the partition function cancel out when reparameterizing Bradley–Terry with the policy ratios?
questions.question_body:
In Eq. (6), the authors substitute the reward reparameterization

$$r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x)$$

into the Bradley–Terry probability $\sigma(r(x,y_1)-r(x,y_2))$. They say the partition function terms cancel, yielding Eq. (7). I see that $\beta \log Z(x)$ appears in both $r(x,y_1)$ and $r(x,y_2)$, but could someone write out the algebra that shows the $\log Z(x)$ terms disappear inside the logistic function and that the result depends only on the log policy ratios?

questions.title: What exactly is $\beta$ controlling in DPO, and how should I pick it to target a desired KL?
questions.question_body: The paper treats $\beta$ as a knob that trades off reward maximization vs staying close to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. In Eq. (8), $\beta$ scales the log ratio terms inside the logistic. Intuitively, smaller $\beta$ should enforce a stronger KL penalty, but the practical mapping from $\beta$ to the realized sequence-level KL is unclear to me. Is there a theoretical relationship between $\beta$ and the expected $\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}[\pi\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}]$ under the Bradley–Terry model? In practice, do people tune $\beta$ by directly monitoring the KL, or is there a heuristic initialization (e.g., matching a target KL via a line search)?

questions.title: How are sequence probabilities computed in Eq. (8) for autoregressive LMs, and does DPO suffer from length bias?
questions.question_body: Eq. (8) uses terms like $\log \pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)$. For an autoregressive LM, is this the sum of token-level log-probabilities along $y$ including an end-of-sequence token, i.e. $\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log \pi_{\theta}(y_t\mid x, y_{<t})$? If yes, does DPO inherit length biases (e.g., longer $y$ accumulating larger-magnitude log-prob sums)? Do we need any normalization (per-token averaging) or special handling (like explicit length penalties or EOS handling) to make the pairwise comparisons in Eq. (8) well-behaved?

questions.title: What assumptions ensure the DPO objective is consistent when preference data come from a different sampling policy?
questions.question_body: The dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of $(x, y_w, y_l)$ pairs is often collected from $\pi^{\text{SFT}}$, but DPO optimizes a new $\pi_\theta$ and uses a designated $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ in the loss. Under what conditions (on coverage, support, or overlap between $\pi^{\text{SFT}}$ and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$) is the maximum-likelihood estimator in Eq. (8) statistically consistent for the optimal policy $\pi^*$? Does severe mismatch between the data-generating policy and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ bias the learned policy, and is the "reference fitting" trick (MLE on $y_w$) sufficient to remove that bias in theory or only as a practical heuristic?

questions.title: Can someone clarify the equivalence classes of rewards and why adding an $f(x)$ term does not change the optimal policy?
questions.question_body: The paper defines an equivalence relation over rewards where $r \sim r'$ if $r(x,y) - r'(x,y) = f(x)$. I understand this keeps Bradley–Terry probabilities the same since differences $r(x,y_1)-r(x,y_2)$ are invariant. But why does this also leave the KL-regularized optimal policy in Eq. (4) unchanged? Is it simply because $\exp((1/\beta)f(x))$ factors into the partition function $Z(x)$ and thus cancels? A short proof sketch for Lemma 2 would help.

questions.title: Does the DPO reparameterization restrict the class of representable rewards (Theorem 1)?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 claims that any reward class consistent with Plackett–Luce/Bradley–Terry can be represented as $r(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$ for some $\pi$. I’m confused about the role of $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ here. If $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ has zero support on certain $(x,y)$ that receive positive reward under the true optimal $\pi_r$, can we still represent the corresponding reward class via the log-ratio form? Are any support or absolute continuity assumptions required for the theorem to hold?

questions.title: Intuition behind the DPO gradient weighting term $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_w))$
questions.question_body: The gradient expression shows DPO upweights examples where the implicit reward $\hat r_\theta$ ranks the losing completion higher than the winner. How should I interpret this compared to vanilla "likelihood up, unlikelihood down"? Is this weighting term equivalent to the negative gradient of logistic regression on the margin $\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)$? Does it have a margin-maximization flavor (like pushing incorrectly ordered pairs more strongly) and is that the main reason DPO avoids degeneration compared to naive unlikelihood training?

questions.title: How do we avoid backpropagating through $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ in practice, and does its parameterization matter?
questions.question_body: Eq. (8) contains $\log \frac{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$. My understanding is that $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is a frozen model used only to compute the denominator’s log-prob. In implementation, do we detach $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ entirely (no gradients)? Also, does it matter if $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ shares the same tokenizer or architecture as $\pi_\theta$? If not, how do we ensure sequence log-probs are comparable (e.g., consistent handling of BOS/EOS, tokenization differences)?

questions.title: Is Eq. (8) equivalent to logistic regression on log-odds features, and what are the implications?
questions.question_body: Rewriting Eq. (8), the argument to $\sigma(\cdot)$ is $\beta[(\log \pi_\theta(y_w\mid x) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)) - (\log \pi_\theta(y_l\mid x) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x))]$. This looks like logistic regression where the "feature" is the difference of log-probability ratios and the model parameter is implicitly $\theta$. Is it valid to interpret DPO as performing logistic regression on the sufficient statistic $\log \pi_\theta(y\mid x) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)$? If so, does that grant convexity in the feature space but non-convexity through $\theta$, and does it explain some of the stability properties the authors observe?

questions.title: What prevents DPO from overfitting to pairwise preferences when multiple good answers exist?
questions.question_body: Bradley–Terry is pairwise and only constrains differences, so if both $y_w$ and $y_l$ are decent but $y_w$ is marginally better, DPO will still push their log-probability ratio. In aggregate, could this collapse diversity by overemphasizing tiny pairwise wins? Are there practical safeguards (e.g., temperature during sampling, early stopping, regularization on $\pi_\theta$, mixing SFT loss) to preserve coverage over multiple high-quality modes?

questions.title: How does DPO handle ranked lists under Plackett–Luce, and what changes in the loss?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions an extension from Bradley–Terry to Plackett–Luce in the appendix. If I have a ranked list $y_{(1)} \succ y_{(2)} \succ \cdots \succ y_{(k)}$, what is the exact DPO loss for that case? Does it factor into a sum of pairwise logistic terms with the same $\beta$ and $\log \pi/\pi_{\text{ref}}$ ratios, or do we need a different normalization to respect the PL likelihood? A concrete formula would help me implement it.

questions.title: What is the precise relationship between DPO and PPO with a learned reward—do they optimize the same fixed point?
questions.question_body: The paper states DPO "optimizes the same objective" as PPO-based RLHF with a KL constraint. However, PPO typically alternates between policy updates and value/baseline estimation and may use clipped objectives. Under idealized assumptions (infinite data, exact optimization, no clipping), do DPO and PPO converge to the same $\pi^*$ that satisfies Eq. (7)? If so, can someone outline a proof sketch that the DPO MLE solution corresponds to the fixed point of the KL-regularized policy improvement used by PPO when the reward comes from Bradley–Terry-consistent preferences?

questions.title: Why do the authors say DPO does not require a baseline term while actor–critic does?
questions.question_body: In Eq. (10), the paper argues that actor–critic methods need a baseline (soft value) to reduce variance, while DPO’s reparameterization avoids this. Could someone explain more concretely why the term $-\beta \log \sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp(\frac{1}{\beta} r_\phi(x,y))$ acts as a baseline in actor–critic, and why optimizing the pairwise logistic in Eq. (8) obviates any separate baseline/value function for variance reduction?

questions.title: How sensitive is DPO to errors in human preference labels, and is there a principled way to model annotator noise?
questions.question_body: Bradley–Terry assumes a logistic link from reward differences to win probabilities. If human labels are noisy or inconsistent, DPO will still fit the implicit reward to match those odds. Are there variants of DPO that incorporate annotator-specific noise models (e.g., temperature per annotator), or robust losses (e.g., label smoothing, margin thresholds) to mitigate the impact of noisy or adversarial comparisons? Would this just correspond to changing the link function or adding per-example weights in Eq. (8)?

questions.title: What happens if $\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)$ is extremely small—does the log-ratio explode?
questions.question_body: Since Eq. (8) uses $\log \frac{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$, if the reference assigns near-zero probability to a completion $y$, the ratio can become very large. Is this a practical problem that causes unstable gradients or encourages the model to exploit rare modes? Do implementations clip $\log \pi_{\text{ref}}$ or add a floor $\epsilon$? How does this interact with the desire for the KL constraint to keep $\pi_\theta$ near $\pi_{\text{ref}}$?

questions.title: Does DPO require on-policy data at any point, or is it purely offline once $\mathcal{D}$ is fixed?
questions.question_body: One big appeal is removing the RL loop. But I want to confirm: after constructing $\mathcal{D}=\{(x,y_w,y_l)\}$ offline (e.g., from $\pi^{\text{SFT}}$), can DPO training proceed entirely offline with no need to resample new pairs from the evolving $\pi_\theta$? If so, are there any known failure modes from distributional shift during training (e.g., learned policy moving into regions unsupported by $\mathcal{D}$) and how are they mitigated?

questions.title: How do we reconcile DPO’s sequence-level loss with token-level training dynamics during backprop?
questions.question_body: Even though Eq. (8) is defined over full sequences $y$, gradients w.r.t. $\theta$ ultimately flow through token-level logits. In practice, are the token-level gradients simply the usual teacher-forced cross-entropy gradients scaled by the logistic weight $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))$ and the $\beta$ factor, applied to $y_w$ with a positive sign and to $y_l$ with a negative sign? Or is there any subtlety with stop-gradients across the two sequences when computing the implicit reward estimates $\hat r_\theta$?
